A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCAR research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, ranking accuracies, stylometric analyses, and ablations across coding and open-ended tasks, including detailed appendix results.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and additionally reports content-only perplexity measurements and conditional mutual information estimates.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same quality-constrained ranking objective, representation branches, triplet regularization, and top-percentage selection procedure. Presentation and creativity styles are renamed linguistic form and semantic surprisal. The new word filtering serves the diagnostic analyses; it is not introduced into the ranker's input pipeline.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same training sources, coding languages, HumanEval/MultiPL-E evaluation, and AlpacaEval tasks. The tulu-v2 and guanaco-commits names in v5 identify the previously evaluated OLMO and StarCoder training datasets. The new diagnostics use existing StackExchange and LIMA coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding selection experiments retain Random, Perplexity, Superfiltering, HFR, AlpaGasus, and Diversity alongside SCAR(ID/OOD). The official OLMO-7b-SFT and Octocoder comparisons also remain. Newly cited approaches are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: v5 substantially revises the operational measurement of the central surprisal factor: the main analysis uses PPL(yc|x) after removing functional words, while retaining code blocks and preserving whole-response measurements in the appendix. It adds a conditional-dependence evaluation protocol. Appendix A.4 also changes reported ranker training from 20 epochs to up to 20 with validation-based early stopping; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 extends the existing style analysis with a conditional mutual information diagnostic of instruction dependence and a comparison of content-only versus whole-response perplexity (Section 2, Appendices A.6–A.8). The component ablations, generator comparisons, cross-domain evaluations, and representation-similarity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.7 introduces a statistical estimation procedure for conditional mutual information using Llama3 probabilities and averaged conditional log-probability ratios. Existing descriptive mean/standard-deviation reporting continues. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests for the performance comparisons.

E6.justification: v5 adds content-only perplexity statistics and CMI findings: semantic/form instruction-dependence estimates are 0.40/0.15 for LIMA and 0.49/0.03 for StackExchange. Most benchmark and ablation scores remain identical. The 5,000-example StarCoder C++ Pass@1/Pass@10 entries change from 34.53/49.90 to 32.83/44.47 (v1 Table 17; v5 Table 18), with Table 5's aggregate changing from 40.98 to 40.09.

T1.justification: v5 introduces the semantic/functional response decomposition and explicit sample-average definitions for two conditional mutual information quantities in Appendix A.7. These extend the mathematical formulation of the diagnostics. The SCAR objectives remain mathematically equivalent, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory framing shift from decomposing response style into two components to identifying two influential stylistic factors, with creativity framed more specifically as semantic predictability. This modestly narrows the conceptual claim. The principal claims about style consistency, SCAR's effectiveness, and successful selection of as little as 0.7% of the data remain.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations of instruction dependence, imperfect semantic/form separation, and the fluency effects of removing functional words. It narrows the quality-constraint benefit to particular lower-quality training conditions. Conversely, v1's dedicated limitation about GPT-3.5-like style bias restricting diverse outputs and role-playing applications is removed rather than relocated.

D1.justification: v5 newly specifies GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4-1106-preview, direct-generation temperature zero, dataset identifiers, and POS/code-block extraction rules. Appendix A.16 clarifies the Octocoder benchmark variant underlying the retained baseline score. Most hardware and fine-tuning settings, generation prompts, and the code/data availability statement were already present.

R1.justification: v5 substantially expands the conceptual positioning of style, explicitly distinguishing its semantics-inclusive account from non-semantic and in-context accounts through discussions of Hovy, Lin, DiMarco and Hirst, and Jin. It also connects the measurement and design choices to surprisal, style-removal, conditional-information, and self-distillation literature, beyond v1's narrower selection/authorship framing.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting extends across the introduction, style definitions, method explanations, results discussion, and appendix commentary. Terminology is standardized, the open-source-model comparison moves into the main-results subsection, and reproducibility and ethics statements are introduced while the dedicated limitations section disappears.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive table relocation and caption revision. Figure 3 reorganizes the same ablations from two panels into four; Figure 1's perplexity plot changes scale and distribution. v5 also adds a word-classification illustration and content-only perplexity columns to the appendix tables.

improvement.justification: v5 improves interpretability and reproducibility through explicit content-only surprisal measurement, additional dependence diagnostics, precise model versions, and clarification of the Octocoder evaluation variant. These address underexplained aspects of v1's measurement and comparison setup. The net gain is limited: the diagnostics still rely on imperfect semantic separation, and removing v1's specific style-bias limitation weakens the discussion of applicability.
